transcript.text: Hi, the light in my Neff oven has stopped working (model B1ACE4HN0B). Oven works fine otherwise. Can I change the bulb myself and what bulb do I need?

Yes, in most cases this is a job you can do yourself. If the oven heats and cooks normally and only the light has gone, it's almost always just a blown bulb, which is a cheap fix. As for which bulb, it has to be a special heat-resistant oven lamp rated to 300°C, never an ordinary household bulb. Neff ovens typically use one of two types:
• a small screw-in bulb (SES/E14, usually 25W) behind a round glass cover at the back of the oven, or
• a G9 halogen capsule (usually 25W or 40W) with two wire loops that push straight in, behind a rectangular glass cover on a side wall. I can't confirm which one your model takes. The safest way to be sure is to take the old bulb out and read the markings on it, so you can match the type, wattage and 300°C rating exactly. Here's how to check and change it:
1. Make sure the oven is completely cold. Switch it off at the wall cooker switch or isolator, not just at the controls. If you can't find an isolator, turn it off at the fuse box.
2. Remove the shelves and lay a folded tea towel on the oven floor to catch the glass cover if it slips.
3. Remove the cover. A round cover at the back usually unscrews anticlockwise, and rubber gloves help with grip if it's stiff. A side cover usually unclips: ease it off gently from the edge with a plastic spatula or a spoon handle, following any notch in the glass.
4. Take the bulb out. An E14 bulb unscrews anticlockwise. A G9 halogen pulls straight out. If the bulb looks blackened or the filament is broken, that suggests it's blown.
5. Fit the new bulb. Hold a halogen bulb with a tissue rather than bare fingers, because skin oil shortens its life. Then refit the cover, making sure any seal is seated, and switch back on. If a new, correct bulb still doesn't light, a couple of less common causes come next. Some ovens only switch the light on with certain functions, when the door is opened, or have a setting that turns it off, so the manual is worth a quick look. Beyond that, it points to the lamp holder or its wiring, or to the door switch. If bulbs keep blowing quickly, the holder is the usual suspect. Both of those mean dismantling the oven, so they're a job for an engineer. It's very unlikely to be the main control board when everything else works. Which kind of cover does yours have: a round one at the back, or a rectangular one on the side?

Thanks, I'll isolate it at the cooker switch and let it cool first. I've already got the glass cover off (round one, came off with a rubber glove). The old bulb says E14, 25W, 300C and the filament looks broken. Is that the right replacement to buy?

Yes. A like-for-like E14 (small screw-in/SES) 25W oven lamp rated to 300°C is exactly what to look for. Matching the markings on the old bulb is the most reliable guide, more so than any listing for the model, which I can't confirm. With a broken filament and the oven otherwise working normally, I'm fairly confident it's simply a blown bulb. When choosing one, make sure the packaging specifically says oven lamp and 300°C. Fridge and appliance bulbs look the same but are only rated for low temperatures and will fail quickly or crack. Clear or frosted glass both work fine. One quick point on order: as the cover is already off, make sure the cooker switch is off before you touch the old bulb or the holder. When you fit it:
1. Screw the new bulb in clockwise until it's just snug. Don't force it, as the ceramic holder can crack.
2. Wipe the glass cover clean, check any seal is sitting properly, and screw it back on firmly by hand.
3. Switch back on at the cooker switch and turn the light or oven on. If it lights, that's the job done. If a new 300°C bulb doesn't light, first check whether the light only comes on with certain functions or when the door is open. After that, the next suspect is the lamp holder or its wiring, which is an engineer job. The same applies if replacement bulbs keep blowing within weeks.
